questions.q: According to this lesson, which of the following is a genuine, legitimate reason to keep a workload on-premises?
options: A hard data-residency requirement that no available cloud region can satisfy
The team has always run it on-prem and prefers not to change
Migrating would require learning a new cloud provider's console
The workload hasn't been reviewed in over a year
questions.explain: A data-residency or regulatory requirement is a real, hard constraint. Habit or unfamiliarity with the target platform are not legitimate justifications under this framework.

questions.q: Which type of workload is specifically called out as a good candidate for moving to the cloud?
options: A workload bound by single-digit-millisecond latency requirements
A workload with variable or unpredictable demand that would be expensive to provision for on fixed on-prem hardware
A regulated workload with a strict data-residency requirement
A legacy system with no remaining in-house expertise and no reliable rollback path
questions.explain: Variable or unpredictable demand is exactly what cloud elasticity is built for, and provisioning fixed on-prem hardware for that pattern is typically wasteful.

questions.q: In the five-question checklist from this lesson, what should you do if a hard latency requirement rules out available cloud deployments?
options: Move the workload anyway and accept the latency increase
Stop at that question — the workload stays local, since no available cloud deployment can meet the latency requirement
Re-run the checklist from question one using a different cloud provider
Treat the latency requirement as irrelevant and proceed to the cost comparison
questions.explain: The checklist is designed to stop at the first question that gives a definite answer — a hard latency constraint that no available deployment can meet settles the decision on its own.

questions.q: What is the 'sunk cost fallacy in reverse' described in this lesson?
options: Assuming a workload should always move to the cloud regardless of its actual requirements
Believing that cloud migration is always cheaper than remaining on-premises
Refusing to migrate a workload because of hardware that was recently purchased
Treating 'we already have the hardware' as a reason to keep something on-prem even after its original justification no longer applies
questions.explain: The lesson specifically defines this as continuing to justify an on-prem decision by existing infrastructure, even once the actual regulatory or latency reason behind it is gone.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue the stay-on-prem-vs-move decision should be revisited on a real cadence rather than treated as permanent?
options: Cloud providers require every workload to be re-evaluated annually by contract
On-premises hardware depreciates fully within exactly one year
A workload's classification never changes once it is decided
The inputs to the decision — regulation, available cloud services, and the business's risk tolerance — change over time even when the workload itself doesn't
questions.explain: A workload that correctly stayed on-prem because of a constraint a service couldn't meet at the time may no longer need to, once the available technology or regulatory landscape shifts.
